title: Recurrent Streptococcus Pneumoniae 23 F meningitis due to cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the ear cannel: a case report
case_prompt:
A 6-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with one week of nausea, vomiting, and headache. Initial outpatient treatment provided no relief, and the symptoms progressed to include fever. There was no history of skull trauma. His family noted a remote history of acute otitis media in infancy and a single episode of acute sinusitis two months earlier. 

On examination, he was lethargic with marked neck stiffness. Brudzinski’s and Kernig’s signs were positive. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 29 190/mm3 with 4 % bands. Lumbar puncture showed a CSF white-cell count of 3240/µL (91 % neutrophils), glucose 55 mg/dL, and protein 160.5 mg/dL. Gram stain of the CSF revealed Streptococcus pneumoniae, and both CSF and blood cultures grew S. pneumoniae serotype 23F. He was treated with vancomycin and cefotaxime; blood and CSF cultures confirmed susceptibility, and vancomycin was continued for 14 days.

Six months earlier, he had a similar episode of pneumococcal meningitis (CSF and blood cultures positive for S. pneumoniae 23F), treated with 14 days of vancomycin without complications. To investigate recurrence, immunologic testing, including complement levels and immunoglobulins, was performed and was normal. A sinus CT scan showed only right-sided maxillary sinusitis without bony defects.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Immunologic deficiency was considered and excluded — “the results showed normal immunity.”
2. Chronic sinusitis–induced bony defect was suspected but ruled out — “sinus CT… without any bony defect.”
3. Acquired CSF leak from skull trauma was unlikely given that “no any history of skull trauma was noted before admission.”
4. Cranial dural fistula was suspected based on pathogen specificity as “pneumoccocus… may suggest cranial dural defects.”
5. Radioisotope cisternography localized the lesion — “radioisotope cisternography showed CSF leaked originating from the right petrooccpital region into the middle ear.”
6. High-resolution CT confirmed bony defects in the petrous temporal bone — “HRCT reports showed focal enlargement of the right facial nerve canal, erosion of the bony canal at geniculate ganglion and tympanic segment… reconstruction HRCT showed multiple bony defect at petrous part of temporal bone.”
7. MRI demonstrated multifocal bony destruction with CSF collection — “MRI reports revealed multifocal bony destruction with CSF collection in the right petrous ridge (near the Meckel cave and facial nerve canal at geniculate body ganglion region)…”
